content: Plasmodium malariae is a parasitic protozoan that is responsible for causing malaria in both humans and dogs. It is closely related to other Plasmodium species, such as Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, which are the primary causes of most malarial infections worldwide. However, Plasmodium malariae is often referred to as causing benign malaria because it is significantly less dangerous compared to the infections caused by P. falciparum or P. vivax. The hallmark clinical feature of P. malariae infection is the recurrence of fever at approximately three-day intervals, a pattern known as quartan fever. This is in contrast to the two-day fever intervals typically seen with other malarial parasites. When examined microscopically, red blood cells (erythrocytes) infected by P. malariae do not become enlarged and may even appear smaller than normal red blood cells. The cytoplasm of the infected cells retains its color, and no dots or stippling are visible on the surface of the cells. The parasite itself is compact, with a small food vacuole. It is uncommon for a single red blood cell to host more than one parasite. A distinctive feature of P. malariae is the presence of band forms, where the parasite stretches across the width of the infected cell in a thick band-like structure. This characteristic is often considered diagnostic for this species. Additionally, large grains of malarial pigment are frequently observed within the parasites, more so than in any other Plasmodium species. P. malariae typically produces eight merozoites during its replication cycle. It is important to note that blood samples containing P. vivax or P. ovale that have been stored in EDTA for more than 30 minutes before preparing a blood film may appear very similar to P. malariae under the microscope.
